As I'm sure you're aware state and local bars have been promoting a policy of increased public access to the courts for everyone regardless of financial status. I receive regular messages by newsletter, BA email and journal articles espousing the virtues of pro bono work, pro se forms and pamphlets, and online resources like LegalZoom and Rocket Lawyer to increase access to legal services. To promote access in Washington State its Supreme Court recently approved the practice of non-lawyers in a limited capacity and selected family law as the initial test area. 7 candidates passed the first series of tests in May and are on their way to obtaining LLLT licenses. Congratulations to them!

The Washington State Bar webpage for LLLT states the LLLT's function:

LLLT can do:

  • Obtain relevant facts from clients,
  • Inform clients about possible implications of the law as applied to their cases,
  • Advise clients on how best to manage their legal action for best results,
  • Prepare clients to represent themselves in court proceedings,
  • Perform legal research to answer clients’ legal questions,
  • Draft legal documents to be filed with the court.

LLLT cannot do:

  • Represent clients in court,
  • Negotiate on behalf of a client, and
  • Can only prepare legal documents that have been approved by the Limited License Legal Technician Board.

Do you think the LLLT is a game changer, or a mere formality of what we have our assistants do already? I think it will actually encourage people to seek legal services who might not otherwise due to the perceived cost, and both full and limited practitioners will benefit as a result. Thoughts?
Lawyers, What do you think of the new Limited License Legal Technician (LLLT) practitioners?

Payment is by client payment of fees directly to the LLLT (I presume). The admission to practice rule reads like they are independently licensed and can set up their own shop without lawyer supervision. See Rule 28 of the State Court Rules, Section F, Scope of Practice Authorized by Limited Practice Rule:

"If the issue is within the defined practice area, the LLLT may undertake the following ... "

Also, Sec.G(3):

"Prior to the performance of the services for a fee, the Limited License Legal Technician shall enter into a written contract with the client, signed by both the client and the Limited License Legal Technician ..."

Rule of Professional Conduct 5.9 says they can also share fees with a lawyer if they want to co-op, which is a big change. Sounds like LLLTs can work for, work with, or be totally independent from licensed attorneys.
